name: Biogas Digesters
summary: Anaerobic digesters that convert organic waste (manure, crop residues) into biogas for cooking and lighting, with nutrient-rich slurry as a by-product for soil fertility.
description: Biogas digesters use anaerobic digestion to break down organic materials — primarily livestock manure, food waste, or agricultural residues — in a sealed chamber. The process produces biogas (typically 60–70% methane) used for cooking, lighting, and potentially electricity generation. The digested slurry remaining after gas production is rich in nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, making it an effective organic fertiliser. In Uganda, two main designs are used: fixed-dome (brick-built, lower maintenance) and floating-drum (metal drum, easier gas pressure management). Household digesters typically range from 4 m³ to 10 m³, requiring 15–30 kg of manure per day. Community or institutional digesters can be 50 m³ or larger. Biogas is particularly well-suited to farming households with livestock, enabling a closed-loop agri-energy system where manure generates fuel and enriched slurry.
applications: Farm lighting (gas lamp or converted to electricity)
Bio-slurry as organic fertiliser for crops
Schools, health centres, and institutional kitchens
benefits: Provides clean cooking fuel, reducing firewood and charcoal use
Nutrient-rich bio-slurry improves soil health and crop yields
Reduces indoor air pollution and associated health risks
Reduces time and cost of firewood collection
Closed-loop system — waste generates productive energy and fertiliser
Long lifespan for fixed-dome designs (15–20 years)
limitations: Requires access to daily supply of livestock manure
Performance dependent on temperature (less effective in cold highland areas)
Initial construction cost can be high for smallholders
Requires regular feeding and maintenance to sustain gas production
Gas pressure can fluctuate depending on design type
operationalNotes: Maintain correct water-to-manure ratio (1:1) for optimum digestion
Feed the digester daily with consistent quantities of manure
Ensure digester is fully sealed — gas leaks reduce output
Allow a 4–6 week initial charging period before expecting gas
Mix hot water into the slurry in cold highland areas to maintain temperature
maintenanceNotes: Inspect inlet and outlet pipes quarterly for blockages
Desludge the digester every 2–3 years to remove accumulated solids
Check gas pipe connections and stove burner nozzles annually
Repaint exterior surfaces of drum-type digesters to prevent rusting
Retrain household members annually on correct operation
